sections.h2: Three ways to sell in Corsicana
sections.html:
In Navarro County you can hire an agent, sell it yourself, or let a cash buyer purchase the house outright. Each trades speed, price and effort differently, so settle which matters most before dialing.

Start by assembling the deed, your latest tax statement, the lender payoff and an honest list of defects. Four documents let any buyer quote fast, and let you compare bids by what you would pocket.

  • Which repairs does the buyer expect before closing?
  • Who pays for the title policy?
  • How many days does the quote stay valid?
  • Insist on every quote in writing.

Corsicana was laid out in 1848, and a railroad and an oil strike in 1894 built much of what you see. Boom periods came in layers, so the housing stock mixes pre-1900 lots near downtown with mid-century streets. Buyers will ask about each house's age, wiring and foundation, and answers backed by receipts go a long way.

The courthouse square anchors the older core. Mention it if you are close, and keep a folder with permits, receipts and any old survey, because a cash buyer cares more about condition and title than about local history.

Navarro County's seat and biggest city, Corsicana, lies about 58 miles southeast of Dallas, where Interstate 45 meets U.S. highways 75 and 287 and State highways 22 and 31. A commute to Dallas along I-45 is a normal selling point. Name the highway access a buyer would use for the daily drive, since small-town shoppers compare that early and it costs you nothing to include.

sections.h2: Which Corsicana projects need a city permit?
sections.html:
Structural work does. The city requires a permit to build, alter, enlarge or repair any home or commercial building within its limits, and the building inspector and Planning and Zoning Department review applications.

Registered contractors pull permits, though a homeowner may pull a homestead permit for personal work. Fees track job value and appear in Chapter 13 of the city code. Contractor registration costs $110 the first year and $55 after that. Inspections are booked by phone by whoever holds the permit, weekdays between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m., and a call before 3 p.m. can often be inspected that same day.

The Community Support Department covers property maintenance, zoning, addressing, fencing and screening, and trash containment. Staff answer complaints, inspect and write citations. They also run the city cemeteries, which include Woodland, Oakwood and Modrell.

  • Cut tall grass and haul away debris.
  • Repair broken fence sections and screening.
  • Make the house number visible from the street.
  • Store trash carts properly.

Got a notice already? Ask the department what must be corrected and by what date, and hand a copy to the title company.

sections.h2: Navarro County taxes and a sale
sections.html:
Every taxable property in the county is valued by Navarro Central Appraisal District, open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The tax assessor sets neither values nor rates.

Values are fixed as of January 1, the same day the year's lien attaches, and bills go delinquent after January 31. A homestead gets $140,000 off its school value, plus $60,000 more for an owner who is 65 or older or disabled. The title company can explain how the year's bill gets divided between you and the buyer.

Probate of a will is open to heirs for four years after a death. Where there is no will and few assets, a small estate affidavit might do the job, and a recorded transfer on death deed sidesteps probate. The Navarro County Clerk can tell you which documents it requires.

Falling behind does not stop you from selling. A lender typically waits until the loan is over 120 days late, allows 20 days to cure, then posts a sale notice at least 21 days before a first-Tuesday auction. Your servicer can supply a payoff.

sections.h2: What a Corsicana cash sale looks like
sections.html:
The buyer walks through, then sends an offer in writing. Once you agree, a title company examines Navarro County records, asks for payoffs and books closing on your chosen date. Since no loan is involved, nothing waits on an appraisal.

Expect a lower price than a retail sale, because the buyer inherits the repairs. You avoid showings, repair haggling and the chance of a financed buyer walking away. Weigh the bid against a listing's net after commission, fixes and the cost of waiting.

Compare your house with sales on its own block rather than citywide. A pre-1900 house near downtown, a mid-century ranch and a newer build answer different questions. The first draws questions about wiring and foundation, the second about plumbing and roofing, and the third about what the builder covered.

A written timeline of work done, with receipts, answers many of those questions before they are asked. Where work is still needed, say so. Buyers discount known problems far less than surprises found at inspection.

Closing means signing the deed and the settlement papers. From the proceeds, the title company retires your mortgage, clears any tax balance and shares the year's bill with the buyer, then pays you the difference. Bring photo ID and all the keys. The Navarro County Clerk then records the deed, and your copy of the settlement statement belongs in your tax file.

sections.h2: Selling a Corsicana rental or vacant house
sections.html:
An empty house draws code notices faster than an occupied one, so check the yard and the exterior regularly while it sits. If a tenant lives there, hand the buyer the lease and the rent record, and say when the term ends. A buyer who understands the occupancy up front is less likely to renegotiate later.

If the house has stood vacant for a while, have the water and power on for the walkthrough and look for roof or plumbing leaks before a buyer's inspector does.

Handle anything code enforcement would flag, because an open notice can add days to a closing. Mow, haul off debris, mend broken fence sections and check that the house number can be read from the street. Close any open permit, and file receipts for roof, wiring and foundation work, so a buyer sees a house that has been cared for.

faqs.q: How soon can a Corsicana house close?
faqs.a: Anywhere from a couple of weeks for a cash purchase to a month or more for a financed sale. Payoff letters, title work and any probate step set the floor, so request those documents on day one. An open permit or a code notice on the lot can also add days.

faqs.q: Is a permit needed for a fence in Corsicana?
faqs.a: Yes. Fences are on the city's permit list, along with accessory buildings, demolition, drive approaches, irrigation systems, signs and moving a structure. Check with the inspection line.

faqs.q: Who files the deed after closing in Corsicana?
faqs.a: The title company usually records it with the Navarro County Clerk, after the deed has been signed and acknowledged before a notary or witnesses.

faqs.q: Will a Corsicana buyer inherit last year's tax bill?
faqs.a: The tax lien forms on January 1 and stays with the property, so closing settles it. Anything delinquent has to be paid for title to be clear.

faqs.q: Can heirs sell an unprobated Corsicana house?
faqs.a: Often a court step comes first. A muniment of title, small estate affidavit or recorded transfer on death deed may work, whereas a bare affidavit of heirship may not satisfy a title insurer.
